summary: Xi and Trump met in Shenzhen and spoke of steadier ties as chip limits loom; Chinese carmakers scale back factory humanoid robots, and youth unemployment eased to 17.2%.
body: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump held formal talks in Shenzhen on Thursday, after sitting together for two hours at Wednesday's APEC welcome banquet.[^1] Trump said the US-China "Board of Trade", a body the two leaders set up in May to manage trade disputes, has brought "greater balance" to the relationship; its first official meeting was held last Friday.[^2] In a live report credited to Reuters, Xi called ties "stable and improving", asked for closer work on AI safety risks, and warned Washington to handle Taiwan carefully.[^3] A first three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin began later on Thursday; no results had been reported at the time of writing.[^3][^4]

Computer chips hang over the talks. Reuters reported before the summit that US lawmakers are pushing for tighter limits on China's access to advanced AI chips after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned, and that a planned US-China channel for reporting serious AI incidents is not working yet.[^5]

On robots, Caixin reports that Chinese carmakers are pulling humanoid robots off assembly lines because of high costs and weak performance, and giving them simpler jobs.[^6] In Wuhan, CBS News visited a centre where more than 100 graduates wear sensor suits so their everyday movements can train robots; the centre's head guesses a robot could work in homes in three to five years, or up to 10.[^7] My read: the robot push is real, but slower than the showroom demos suggest.

For young people, official data reported this week show unemployment among urban 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in school fell to 17.2% in October from 18% in September; for ages 25 to 29 it was 7.3%.[^8]
differences: Trump says the Board of Trade has made US-China trade fairer; economists cited by Reuters warn his tariff approach could raise prices and widen a trade war.[^2] On robots, Elon Musk has predicted over a billion humanoids within 10 years, as CBS notes, while the Wuhan centre's head expects homes to wait 3 to 10 years and Caixin reports carmakers scaling back.[^6][^7]

reads.title: Inside China's relentless race to develop humanoid robot helpers and get them into our homes
reads.summary: A look inside a Wuhan centre where young graduates act out chores so robots can learn them, and why home robots are still years away.
